title: Inner Compass
definition: The nervous system's continuous orientation between safety and threat, understood through the metaphor of a compass needle that moves fluidly between Connection and Protection.
summary: The Inner Compass is TEG-Blue's core visual-conceptual tool. Like a fluid compass, the needle is constantly moving — it does not have a 'correct' position, it points in a direction. A fluid compass moves between Connection and Protection as conditions change. A stuck compass is one where the needle has lost its capacity to move. Health is not where the needle is, but whether it can move.

content.title: What It Is
content.content: The Inner Compass is the metaphor TEG-Blue uses to make the nervous system's continuous safety-threat orientation visible and clinically usable. The compass needle moves through four positions — Connection, Protection, Control, Domination — along a continuous gradient. A fluid compass has access to the full range. A stuck compass is locked at one position, and the person does not experience it as being stuck — they experience it as 'just who I am.'

content.title: How TEG-Blue Maps It
content.content: The compass reframes health from a state to a capacity. Most models ask 'which state is the person in?' The compass asks 'can the needle move?' This makes 'stuck versus fluid' the primary question rather than mode position. The compass needle moves through a five-step sequence (Perception → Neuroception → Emotion → Autonomic Response → Mode Activation) that typically completes before conscious awareness begins. By the time conscious awareness registers 'an emotion,' the compass needle has already moved.

content.title: Research Basis
content.content: Porges, S. W. (2011) — autonomic states as continuous orientation. Bowlby, J. (1969) — attachment system as safety-seeking orientation. Fredrickson, B. L. (2001) — broaden-and-build as directional state. Siegel, D. J. (2012) — window of tolerance as range of fluid movement. Ogden, P. (2006) — sensorimotor psychotherapy, tracking body-level orientation.
